tagline: Capacity that follows real demand, sized from traffic data rather than a guess.
overview: Two failure modes cost money in opposite directions. Running flat out with no headroom means the next traffic spike becomes an outage; running everything at three times peak means paying for servers that idle most of the year. We size capacity from your actual traffic history and then let it move with demand.

Autoscaling is a control problem, not a switch. Node pools, container replicas and queue consumers all react on different timescales, and a scaler that reacts faster than the application can start will simply thrash. We tune thresholds, cooldowns and warm capacity together, and leave alerts that tell you when scaling is not keeping up.
problems: We over-provision all year to survive one peak
Capacity planning is done in a spreadsheet nobody trusts
Scaling reacts too late, after users have already suffered
No idea which service consumes most of the headroom

includes.title: Scaling policies
includes.text: Horizontal pod, node pool and server group policies tuned to your workload, with sensible cooldowns so the system settles instead of oscillating.

includes.title: Event-driven scaling
includes.text: KEDA and queue-length triggers scale workers on backlog rather than CPU, which suits batch, consumer and asynchronous jobs far better than a processor threshold.

includes.title: Traffic-based sizing
includes.text: We model capacity from historical request rates, including your true daily and seasonal peaks, so the baseline is defensible rather than a number someone liked.

includes.title: Scheduled and predictive scaling
includes.text: Where demand is predictable — a morning login surge, a nightly batch window — we pre-warm capacity on a schedule so scaling never has to race the traffic.

includes.title: Cost and capacity reports
includes.text: Per-service utilisation and headroom reported together, which shows where money is being spent on capacity that is never used.

includes.title: Load testing links
includes.text: Scaling policies are validated against the load tests in your environment, so behaviour under a spike is observed before it happens for real.

deliverables: Capacity model built from historical traffic data
Scaling policy configuration for every workload tier
Kubernetes HPA and node pool definitions in Git
Headroom and utilisation report per service
Documented cooldown and warm-up settings per tier

process.title: Collect the real numbers
process.text: We pull request rates, queue depths and resource usage over the last year to find the genuine peaks rather than the remembered ones.

process.title: Model required capacity
process.text: From that data we build a per-service model of steady state and peak, including the headroom needed for a failed node or zone.

process.title: Implement scaling policies
process.text: Policies are written as code, tested against a synthetic spike in a non-production environment, then rolled out with conservative limits first.

process.title: Watch and adjust
process.text: We review scaling events after a month, remove the policies that never trigger, and tune the ones that fire constantly without adding capacity.

faqs.q: Will autoscaling make our bill unpredictable?
faqs.a: Some variability is the point, but we cap it. You set maximum replica counts and node pool sizes, and we add budget alerts so a runaway scaler is noticed the same day rather than at the end of the month.

faqs.q: Our database is the bottleneck, not the app. Does this help?
faqs.a: Only partly. Scaling stateless application tiers is straightforward; stateful tiers need connection pooling, read replicas and query tuning, and scaling the app harder will just overload the database faster. We will say so if that is the real constraint.

faqs.q: How do you pick thresholds without guessing?
faqs.a: From measurements. We hold the load tests steady at known request rates and watch where latency and saturation start to climb, then set thresholds below that knee rather than at an arbitrary percentage.

faqs.q: Why do we still fall over at peak if we already autoscale?
faqs.a: That usually means something upstream is fixed: a connection limit, a single-writer database, or a warm-up time longer than the burst. Scaling the tier in front of it just moves the queue somewhere else.

seo.title: Autoscaling & Capacity Planning — Sizing From Real Data
seo.description: Traffic-based capacity models and scaling policies that follow your demand, cut idle spend and keep headroom for the peaks you genuinely see.
